questions.question: How does thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) work?
expected_points: Triplet excitons are converted to singlets by thermally activated reverse intersystem crossing (RISC), then emit as delayed fluorescence.
This requires a very small singlet-triplet energy gap (Delta E_ST); the RISC rate follows a Boltzmann factor exp(-Delta E_ST / kT).
A small Delta E_ST is obtained by separating HOMO and LUMO, e.g. with donor-acceptor molecular design.

questions.question: how does thermaly activted delayed florescence work
expected_points: Triplets convert to singlets by thermally activated reverse intersystem crossing (RISC).
Requires a very small singlet-triplet energy gap (Delta E_ST).

questions.question: How can a purely organic emitter without heavy metals turn its dark triplet excitons into light?
expected_points: Through TADF: thermally activated reverse intersystem crossing from T1 to S1 followed by delayed fluorescence.
Requires a small singlet-triplet gap obtained by HOMO/LUMO separation (donor-acceptor design).

questions.question: In TADF emitters, why must ΔEST be small?
expected_points: RISC from T1 to S1 is thermally activated, with a rate proportional to exp(-Delta E_ST / kT), so a small gap makes up-conversion fast.
Small Delta E_ST comes from spatially separating HOMO and LUMO.

questions.question: What causes efficiency roll-off in phosphorescent OLEDs at high current density?
expected_points: Triplet-triplet annihilation (TTA).
Triplet-polaron annihilation (TPA).
Loss of charge balance (and possibly field-induced quenching) at high current.

questions.question: what causes efficency rolloff in phosphorecent OLED at high curent density
expected_points: Triplet-triplet annihilation (TTA).
Triplet-polaron annihilation (TPA).
Loss of charge balance at high current.

questions.question: Why does a phosphorescent OLED become less efficient when I drive it at high brightness?
expected_points: Bimolecular quenching at high exciton/polaron density: TTA and TPA.
Charge imbalance at high current.

questions.question: Why do TTA and TPA matter for PHOLED efficiency at high current?
expected_points: TTA and TPA are annihilation processes that quench triplets when exciton and polaron densities are high.
They are the main causes of efficiency roll-off in phosphorescent OLEDs.

questions.question: What are typical electron mobility values of common amorphous electron transport materials like Alq3?
expected_points: Alq3 and anthracene derivatives (e.g. ADN) have electron mobilities around 1e-7 to 1e-5 cm^2/Vs.
This is at least an order of magnitude lower than the hole mobilities of common hole transporters (about 1e-5 to 1e-3 cm^2/Vs).

questions.question: typical electorn mobilty of Alq3 ETL?
expected_points: Alq3 electron mobility is roughly 1e-7 to 1e-5 cm^2/Vs, lower than typical hole mobilities.

questions.question: What is the role of a charge generation layer in a tandem OLED?
expected_points: It connects stacked emitting units and generates electron-hole pairs, injecting electrons and holes into the adjacent units.
Stacking raises current efficiency/luminance at the same current, which helps with voltage-drop issues in large displays.
Example: n-doped (Cs3PO4:BCP) / p-doped (MoO3:NPD) CGLs.

questions.question: What does a CGL do in a tandem OLED?
expected_points: A charge generation layer generates and injects electrons and holes into neighboring stacked units so they operate in series.

questions.question: How was the lifetime of blue phosphorescent OLEDs improved by reducing triplet-polaron annihilation?
expected_points: A graded dopant concentration profile in a broadened emissive layer lowers the exciton density.
Lower exciton density suppresses triplet-polaron annihilation, giving a more than threefold lifetime improvement.
Combined with a stacked (tandem) structure, the lifetime improved about tenfold.

questions.question: why do blue ones die so fast and how do you fix it?
expected_points: Blue (phosphorescent) OLEDs have short lifetimes because high-energy excitons/polarons drive degradation such as exciton-polaron (triplet-polaron) annihilation.
Lowering exciton density, e.g. graded doping in a broadened emissive layer or stacked devices, extends lifetime.
expected_sources: Chemical degradation mechanisms of highly efficient blue

questions.question: Why do electrically doped (p-i-n) transport layers lower the operating voltage of OLEDs?
expected_points: Doping raises the conductivity of the transport layers, so ohmic losses are small and the bands are nearly flat.
The operating voltage approaches the photon energy of the emitted light.
Doping also improves injection at the contacts (thin depletion layer / better energetic alignment).

questions.question: Why use a PIN structure in OLEDs?
expected_points: Doped (p- and n-type) transport layers give high conductivity and efficient injection, enabling low operating voltage and high power efficiency.

questions.question: Why is the external quantum efficiency of a typical OLED limited to about 20-25%?
expected_points: Most generated light is trapped inside the device, so outcoupling efficiency is only about 20-25%.
Light is lost to waveguide modes, substrate modes, and surface plasmon polariton (SPP) modes at the metal cathode.
High-index organic/ITO layers (n about 1.8-2) versus glass (n about 1.5) cause the trapping.

questions.question: Where does most of the light generated inside an OLED get lost?
expected_points: Waveguide modes in the organic/ITO layers, substrate modes in the glass, and surface plasmon modes at the metal cathode; only about 20-25% escapes.

questions.question: how do I get more light out?
expected_points: Improve outcoupling: e.g. microlens arrays/scattering layers, low-index grids or low-index layers, horizontally oriented emitters, reducing SPP losses.

questions.question: How do residual gases like water vapor during vacuum deposition affect OLED lifetime?
expected_points: Residual water vapor during fabrication reduces device lifetime.
Water introduces changes in electrical characteristics (e.g. series resistance / voltage rise).
Alq3 can decompose by an electrochemical reaction with intercalated water.
expected_sources: Performance and lifetime of vacuum deposited

questions.question: effect of residual water vapour in evaporation chamber on oled life time
expected_points: Water vapor present during deposition shortens OLED lifetime and changes electrical behaviour.
expected_sources: Performance and lifetime of vacuum deposited

questions.question: What exciplex-forming co-host was used to make red phosphorescent OLEDs with both high efficiency and long lifetime?
expected_points: A co-host of the hole transporter NPB and the electron transporter PO-T2T, which forms an exciplex.
Many earlier exciplex co-host OLEDs were efficient but had short operational lifetime; this one achieved both.

questions.question: Is the 25% limit a real thing?
expected_points: Spin statistics: electron-hole recombination forms 25% singlets and 75% triplets, so conventional fluorescent OLEDs are limited to 25% internal quantum efficiency.
The limit is overcome by phosphorescent emitters, TADF, or TTA.

questions.question: How does electron mobility in the electron transport layer influence the operational lifetime of an OLED?
expected_points: Common ETLs have low electron mobility (about 1e-7 to 1e-5 cm^2/Vs), much lower than hole mobilities.
Mobility affects charge balance, which shifts the recombination zone / exciton distribution.
Charge imbalance and recombination near interfaces or blocking layers accelerate degradation; surplus carriers damage materials, so balance improves lifetime.

questions.question: Why can a low-refractive-index electron transport layer raise EQE, and which optical loss channel does it reduce?
expected_points: Loss to the surface plasmon polariton (SPP) mode at the metal cathode depends on the dielectric constant of the ETL, so a low-index ETL reduces SPP (and waveguide) losses.
Low-index ETLs (e.g. PO-T2T) enabled EQE around 34% in sky-blue phosphorescent OLEDs.

questions.question: How does triplet-triplet annihilation raise the efficiency limit of fluorescent OLEDs, while also causing roll-off in phosphorescent OLEDs?
expected_points: In fluorescent OLEDs, TTA fuses two triplets into a singlet (delayed fluorescence), raising the maximum IQE from 25% to about 62.5% (25% + 37.5%).
In phosphorescent OLEDs, TTA quenches emissive triplets at high density, causing efficiency roll-off.
expected_sources: Triplet–triplet annihilation in highly efficient fluorescent

What is an exciton in an organic semiconductor?
expected_points: An exciton is a bound electron-hole pair formed when an electron and a hole recombine (or when a molecule is excited).
Excitons in organic semiconductors are tightly bound (Frenkel-like) and stable at room temperature, largely because of the low dielectric constant.

questions.question: What are hole and electron blocking layers used for in an OLED?
expected_points: Hole and electron blocking layers confine holes and electrons in the emission layer.
This improves the charge balance factor, to which the external efficiency is directly proportional.

questions.question: What is the internal quantum efficiency of an OLED?
expected_points: Internal quantum efficiency (IQE) is the number of photons generated inside the device per injected charge carrier (electron).
External quantum efficiency equals IQE multiplied by the light outcoupling efficiency.

questions.question: How much longer can a tandem OLED last than a single-unit OLED?
expected_points: With N stacked units, the same luminance needs about 1/N of the current density, giving an operational lifetime at least N times longer.
Tsujimura cites 2.82 times the lifetime for a two-stack and 5.20 times for a three-stack tandem OLED.

questions.question: What is the maximum internal quantum efficiency of a fluorescent OLED that uses triplet-triplet annihilation?
expected_points: TTA can raise the singlet yield from 25% to at most 62.5% (25% + 75%/2).
This limit is lower than the 100% reachable with phosphorescence or TADF.

questions.question: Which acceptor was used to p-dope the hole transport layer in the low-voltage pin OLEDs from Leo's group?
expected_points: F4-TCNQ (tetrafluoro-tetracyanoquinodimethane), a very strong acceptor, was used as the p-dopant.
expected_sources: Low-voltage organic electroluminescent devices using pin

questions.question: Compare how phosphorescent emitters and TADF emitters harvest triplet excitons.
expected_points: Phosphorescent emitters contain heavy metals (Ir, Pt) whose strong spin-orbit coupling allows fast intersystem crossing and emission from the triplet state.
TADF emitters convert triplets to singlets by thermally activated reverse intersystem crossing, which needs a very small singlet-triplet gap, and emit delayed fluorescence.
Both can in principle reach 100% internal quantum efficiency.

questions.question: Which optical modes trap light inside an OLED, and how do microlens arrays help extract it?
expected_points: Light is trapped in substrate modes (total internal reflection at the glass/air interface), waveguide modes (high-index organic/ITO layers), and surface plasmon polariton modes at the metal cathode.
Microlens arrays on the substrate extract substrate modes.
Microlens arrays designed for individual pixels can also help extract waveguided and SPP modes.
expected_sources: Recent Advances in OLED Optical Design

questions.question: How does horizontal emitter dipole orientation affect light outcoupling, and how large was the efficiency gain reported for oriented fluorescent emitters?
expected_points: The orientation of emissive molecules strongly affects outcoupling efficiency; horizontally oriented dipoles couple more light out.
In fluorescent small-molecule OLEDs, about 88% horizontal dipoles (vs 66% for isotropic) gave a 1.45-fold efficiency increase.

questions.question: Why do blue phosphorescent OLEDs degrade quickly, and how does a tandem structure extend OLED lifetime?
expected_points: Blue PhOLED degradation is attributed in part to triplet-polaron quenching that creates high-energy polarons and traps; the blue emitter FIrpic is known to be relatively unstable (ligand dissociation).
A tandem OLED reaches the same luminance at a lower current density, so its lifetime is extended (at least N times for N units).

questions.question: What is the difference between triplet-triplet annihilation and triplet-polaron annihilation in phosphorescent OLEDs?
expected_points: In triplet-triplet annihilation two triplets interact (T1 + T1 -> S1 + S0), and one triplet is lost; it is a second-order (quadratic) process in excitation density.
In triplet-polaron annihilation a triplet exciton is quenched by a charge carrier (polaron).
Baldo et al. found triplet-polaron annihilation could not explain the quenching in PtOEP:CBP, which follows a quadratic dependence.
expected_sources: Efficiency Roll-Off in Organic Light-Emitting Diodes

questions.question: How does an exciplex-forming co-host lower the driving voltage and reduce efficiency roll-off in phosphorescent OLEDs?
expected_points: Charge carriers recombine in the exciplex host by Langevin recombination and energy is transferred to the emitter, instead of trap-assisted recombination on the dopant.
This gives low charge density and fewer polarons, reducing triplet-polaron quenching and roll-off.
Exciplex-host devices show low turn-on voltages (e.g. 2.6 V for mCBP:PO-T2T).

questions.question: What device structure gives an OLED several times the operational lifetime by stacking emission units, and what layer connects those units?
expected_points: The tandem (stacked) OLED: N units reach the same luminance at about 1/N of the current density, so the lifetime is extended about N times.
The units are connected by a charge generation layer (CGL) that generates electrons and holes and injects them into the adjacent units.

questions.question: Which blue phosphorescent emitter was doped at 10 wt% in the sky-blue OLED with 34.1% EQE, and why is that emitter considered unstable?
expected_points: The emitter is FIrpic.
FIrpic is known to be relatively unstable: its picolinate ligand can split off (reversible) or lose CO2 (irreversible), and the fragments can act as exciton quenchers.

questions.question: Which phosphorescent dye did Baldo's transient analysis of triplet-triplet annihilation study in CBP, and how did its quenching depend on excitation intensity?
expected_points: The dye was PtOEP (platinum octaethylporphyrin) doped in CBP (and Alq3).
Its triplets show intensity-dependent quenching consistent with triplet-triplet annihilation, a second-order process; simple TTA predictions fail at low PtOEP concentrations.

questions.question: What strong acceptor was used to p-dope the hole transport layer in the low-voltage pin OLED, and why does doping the transport layers allow efficient injection despite energy barriers?
expected_points: The p-dopant was F4-TCNQ.
Doping creates thin space-charge layers at the contacts, so carriers tunnel into the transport layers (efficient tunneling injection) and the voltage drop is low.
expected_sources: Low-voltage organic electroluminescent devices using pin
